sections.title: Masses and Springs · Theory and Prediction
One mass, two directions

teaching.text: A mass on a spring has a resting place called **equilibrium**. When the mass is moved away from that place, the spring is stretched or squeezed, and it pulls or pushes the mass back. That pull toward rest is the **restoring force**.
children: The restoring force gets the mass moving toward rest.
The mass has **inertia**, so it does not stop at rest. It keeps going and bends the spring the other way.

teaching.text: Now the spring pulls in the opposite direction. The mass slows down, turns around and comes back.
children: This happens again and again.
A movement that repeats around a resting place is called an **oscillation**.

teaching.text: The mass can swing in two directions.
children: In **longitudinal motion**, it moves along the spring, so the spring gets longer and shorter.
In **transverse motion**, it moves across the spring. The spring is already pulled tight, so when the mass moves off the line, the spring tilts and pulls it back.

teaching.text: Both directions repeat at the same **frequency**, which is the number of cycles in each second.
children: They match because the mass is the same and the spring is equally stiff in both directions.
The direction of motion changes how the spring pulls, but it does not change how fast the cycle repeats.

sections.title: Mass and stiffness change the rate

teaching.text: Two things set how fast a mass on a spring swings. One is the **mass** itself, and the other is the **stiffness** of the spring. Each comparison changes only one of them, so its effect stands out clearly.
**A heavier mass swings more slowly.**
children: A heavy mass is harder to speed up and harder to stop.
The same spring needs more time to turn it around, so each cycle takes longer.
Making the mass **four times** heavier cuts the frequency **in half**.

teaching.text: **A stiffer spring makes the mass swing faster.**
children: A stiff spring pulls back harder for the same stretch.
The mass turns around sooner, so more cycles fit into each second.
Making the spring **four times** stiffer **doubles** the frequency.

teaching.text: Mass and stiffness work against each other.
children: Mass resists changes in motion.
Stiffness drives the mass back toward rest.

teaching.text: Speed of repetition is a separate thing from size of swing.
children: How far the mass moves is its **amplitude**. A big swing is not necessarily a fast one.
Frequency comes from counting full cycles over the same amount of time.

teaching.text: The sideways and lengthwise versions match because each one has the same **effective stiffness** in its own direction of motion. For sideways motion, that stiffness comes from how tightly the spring is stretched.

sections.title: Two masses have two normal modes

teaching.text: With two equal masses held between fixed walls, the system has **two normal modes**. A **normal mode** is a pattern where every part moves at the same rate and keeps the same relationship to the others.
In **Mode 1**, the two masses move together in the same direction.
children: The space between them hardly changes.
The spring in the middle barely stretches, so the pull back is weaker and this mode is slower.

teaching.text: In **Mode 2**, the masses move toward each other and then apart.
children: The middle spring now stretches and squeezes hard.
That extra pull makes this mode faster, though not exactly twice as fast.

teaching.text: Both masses take part in both modes.
children: The parts are the same in each mode.
What changes is how the masses move relative to each other, together in one mode and opposed in the other.

teaching.text: The two modes can also happen at the same time.
children: At each mass, the two movements simply add. Where they push the same way, they build up, and where they push opposite ways, they cancel.
This adding is called **superposition**. The combined motion looks uneven, but it holds both frequencies at once.

sections.title: Pop quiz
Three masses have three normal modes

teaching.text: Three equal masses between fixed walls have **three normal modes**, one for each mass that can move.
In **Mode 1**, all three masses move the same way.
children: The middle mass moves the most, and the outer masses move less.
Neighbors are not working against each other, so the springs stretch only a little. This is the slowest mode.

teaching.text: In **Mode 2**, the two outer masses move in opposite directions, and the middle mass stays still.
children: The pulls on the middle mass from each side are equal and opposite, so they cancel.
A point that stays still during a mode is called a **node**.

teaching.text: In **Mode 3**, the outer masses move together, and the middle mass moves the other way.
children: Every mass is now working against its neighbor, so every spring stretches hard.
This is the fastest mode.

teaching.text: The rule behind the order is simple.
children: The more neighbors move against each other, the more the springs stretch.
More stretching means a stronger pull back, and a stronger pull back means a faster mode.

teaching.text: The same three masses move in every mode.
children: When all three modes happen together, their movements add at each mass.
The middle mass still moves in the mixture, because the first and third modes move it even though the second does not.

sections.title: One more mass, one more mode

teaching.text: A chain gains one more **normal mode** for every mass that can move. A chain of one mass has one mode, and a chain of six masses has six.
In every chain, **Mode 1** is the simplest pattern, with all the masses moving together.
children: Each higher mode adds one more group that moves the opposite way.
More groups moving against each other means more springs being stretched.
That gives a stronger pull back and a faster rate.

teaching.text: The two ends of the chain are fixed, so they never move.
children: Inside a chain, a mass can stay still in one mode. That still point is a **node** of that mode, while the rest of the chain keeps moving.
A higher mode uses the very same masses and springs. Only the pattern of movement changes.

teaching.text: The size of a movement and the rate of a movement are different things.
children: **Amplitude** is how far the parts move.
Frequency is how often the movement repeats. A tall pattern is not necessarily a fast one.

teaching.text: Chains made of separate masses do not have the perfectly even, whole-number spacing of frequencies that an ideal string has.

sections.title: A fixed–fixed string combines harmonics

teaching.text: A **fixed–fixed string** is held still at both ends, so both ends are **nodes**. The string can only vibrate in shapes that fit whole half-waves between its ends.
children: The first mode fits one half-wave, a single arch.
Each higher mode fits one more half-wave.

teaching.text: More half-waves in the same length means shorter waves.
children: At the same speed, shorter waves repeat faster.
The modes run at **100, 200, 300, 400 and 500 Hz**.

teaching.text: The lowest frequency is the **fundamental**.
children: The others are exact whole-number multiples of it.
Frequencies spaced this way are called **harmonics**.

teaching.text: One string can carry all of these modes at the same time.
children: At each point along the string, the movements add. Some build up, and some cancel.
The overall shape keeps changing, but each mode inside it stays regular. A point can look still for a moment and then move strongly again, and every mode is still there.

teaching.text: A **pickup** records the motion at one point on the string.
children: Its **spectrum** has one peak for each mode, at that mode’s frequency.
The modes were tuned to give equal peaks at that one point. At a different point, the peaks would have different heights.

sections.title: A membrane combines spatial modes

teaching.text: A **membrane** is a vibrating surface with fixed edges. A surface spreads in two directions, so each mode is named with two numbers. Each number counts the moving regions in one direction.
children: In **(1,1)**, the whole surface moves as one region.
In **(2,1)** and **(1,2)**, the surface splits into two regions, in one direction or the other.
In **(2,2)**, it splits into four regions, and in **(3,1)**, into three in a row.

teaching.text: Regions that sit next to each other always move in opposite directions.
children: The lines between them stay still. These still lines are **nodes**.
The outer edges stay still too, because they are fixed.

teaching.text: All the modes can happen at once, and their movements add at every point.
children: Some places build up and others cancel, so the whole surface keeps changing shape.

teaching.text: A node stays still the whole time.
children: A moving region also passes through the flat resting level, but only for an instant on its way past. That passing moment does not make it a node.
The two numbers describe how the surface divides. They are not two separate frequencies.

teaching.text: A **pickup** at one point gives a spectrum with one peak for each mode.
children: The frequencies here were **picked for teaching** and spaced evenly. A real rectangle would have its own natural frequencies, so the even spacing models how frequencies combine rather than how every membrane behaves.

sections.title: Theory makes a measurable prediction

teaching.text: Science depends on stating very clear theories about how the world works. In this field, those theories are usually written as **differential equations**.
children: A differential equation describes how the parts of a system change over time.
Solving it gives a **prediction**, a statement of what a real measurement should show.

teaching.text: The theory here is that the **vocal folds are a membrane**.
children: A vibrating membrane makes a wave whose spectrum has **evenly spaced peaks**.
These evenly spaced peaks are called **harmonics**.

teaching.text: The theory leads to a clear prediction.
children: If someone’s **laryngeal vibration** is measured, its spectrum should have **equidistant harmonics**, with equal gaps between the peaks.
The test is to record real vocal-fold vibration and look at how its peaks are spaced.
Even spacing would support the theory. Uneven spacing would count against it.

teaching.text: The spacing is what makes the prediction a real test.
children: The vocal folds vibrate in any case, so seeing vibration alone settles nothing.
The membrane animation used frequencies that were chosen to be even, so it pictures the idea but cannot test it. A recording of a real voice is what can test it.

sections.title: One fixed end and one free end

teaching.text: A **fixed–free system** is held at one end and free at the other. Each end sets a rule for every shape the system can take.
children: The fixed end must be a **node**, a point that does not move.
The free end must be an **antinode**, the point that moves the most.

teaching.text: The shapes that follow both rules fit odd numbers of **quarter-waves**.
children: The simplest shape fits one quarter-wave. It is still at the fixed end and swings most at the free end.
The next shapes fit three, five and seven quarter-waves.
These are the **first, third, fifth and seventh harmonics**. So the second allowed mode is the third harmonic, not the second.

teaching.text: Even numbers of quarter-waves are not allowed.
children: An even number would put a still point at the free end, which breaks the rule for that end.
Higher modes fit shorter waves into the same length, so they repeat faster.

teaching.text: The antinode does not stay at its farthest point.
children: It swings through rest to the other side on each cycle.
The fixed end stays still the whole time.

teaching.text: The fixed–fixed and fixed–free examples were tuned separately to share the same lowest frequency.
children: If only one end were freed, with nothing else changed, the lowest frequency would drop **by half**.

sections.title: Masses and Springs in Speech Production
Dynamic systems in economic stabilization

teaching.text: A **dynamic system** is a system that changes over time because its parts affect each other. The idea is not limited to springs. Economists use it to describe how a whole economy rises and falls.
children: **Woodford’s theory**, called **Dynamic Stochastic General Equilibrium** or **DSGE**, treats the economy this way.
The name means the economy changes over time, gets hit by random shocks and has many linked markets that move toward balance together.

teaching.text: Two quantities matter here, **unemployment** and **inflation**.
children: Without stabilization, both swing up and down in large, sharp jumps.
With stabilization, the swings become smaller and smoother.

teaching.text: **Stabilization** means making the swings smaller.
children: The economy still changes over time.
The goal is to avoid harmful extremes, like very high unemployment or inflation that runs out of control.

teaching.text: A spring and an economy share one basic question. What causes the swings, and what can calm them down?
children: In a spring, inertia and the restoring force keep the mass moving back and forth.
In an economy, shocks and the way its parts respond keep the numbers moving up and down.

sections.title: Mass, stiffness, position, and frequency

teaching.text: The behavior of these systems comes down to a short list of **principles of mass–spring systems**.
The first two are about the whole system.
children: **More mass lowers the frequency, and more stiffness raises it.** A heavy load is slow to turn around, and a stiff spring pulls back hard.
**A system with n masses has n modes**, and each mode is faster than the one before it.

teaching.text: The next three say that **location matters**.
children: Added mass lowers a mode’s frequency only as much as that mass actually moves in the mode.
Added stiffness raises a mode’s frequency only as much as that spring actually stretches or squeezes.
Movement and stretching peak in different places. Where parts move the most, they move together, so nothing stretches. Where stretching is greatest, the middle point hardly moves.

teaching.text: So the same change can matter a lot in one mode and very little in another.
children: A spot that swings widely in a mode feels added mass strongly.
A spot that stays still in a mode barely feels it.

teaching.text: The last two are about the ends of the system.
children: When **both ends are fixed**, the harmonics are whole-number multiples of the lowest frequency.
When **one end is fixed and one is free**, the harmonics are **odd multiples** of the lowest frequency.

sections.title: A local change affects two modes differently

teaching.text: This **pop quiz** asks what happens when mass or stiffness is added at one spot on a string, and how that change affects **Mode 4** and **Mode 5**.
The two modes use that spot in different ways.
children: In **Mode 4**, the spot swings strongly. Its neighbors swing with it, so the string there hardly stretches.
In **Mode 5**, the spot barely moves. Its neighbors move differently, so the string there stretches a lot.

teaching.text: **Adding mass** works through movement.
children: In Mode 4, the extra mass gets carried through a big swing, so the mode slows down.
In Mode 5, the spot hardly moves, so the extra mass has almost no effect.
Mass only lowers the frequency when the mass is moving.

teaching.text: **Adding stiffness** works through stretching.
children: In Mode 5, the string at the spot stretches a lot, so a stiffer spring there makes the mode faster.
In Mode 4, the string at the spot barely stretches, so the extra stiffness has little effect.

teaching.text: Adding **both** at once **lowers Mode 4 and raises Mode 5**.
children: The spot is the same in both modes.
What differs is its job. In one mode it mostly swings, and in the other it mostly stretches.

sections.title: Air in a fixed–free tube has modes

teaching.text: The air in the vocal tract can be pictured as a chain of masses joined by springs.
children: Moving air has **inertia**, so it tends to keep moving. That is the mass.
Squeezed air pushes back. That is the spring.
The air moves **back and forth** along the tube, around its usual place. It does not stream steadily out of the mouth.

teaching.text: The tube has one fixed end and one free end.
children: The **glottis** is the fixed end, where the air has little room to move.
The open **lips** are the free end, where the air moves most easily.

teaching.text: The two slowest patterns of this tube match the first two formants.
children: **Mode 1 is like F1**, the lowest resonance.
**Mode 2 is like F2**, with one more back-and-forth reversal inside the tube.
In a perfectly even tube, Mode 2 runs **three times** as fast as Mode 1. A different tube shape changes that.

teaching.text: Each mode is one pattern of motion shared by the whole column of air.
children: In some places, neighboring bits of air move together.
In other places, the gaps between them keep opening and closing.

teaching.text: Three vowels narrow the tube at three places.
children: **/a/** narrows it about **one-third** of the way up from the glottis.
**/i/** narrows it about **two-thirds** of the way up.
**/u/** narrows it at the **lips**.
Mass matters where a mode moves, and springiness matters where it squeezes. So one narrowing can push F1 and F2 in different directions.

sections.title: Vowel shape locates a constriction

teaching.text: Vowels are usually described by **tongue height** and by whether the tongue is **front or back**. Each vowel also narrows the airway at one particular place.
The two high vowels narrow the airway in different places.
children: **Dean** is **high and front**. It narrows about **two-thirds** of the way from the glottis to the lips.
**Dune** is **high and back**. It narrows at the **lips**.
They are both high, but their tract shapes are different.

teaching.text: The two low vowels are at the bottom.
children: **Dan** is **low and front**.
**Don** is **low and back**. It narrows about **one-third** of the way from the glottis.

teaching.text: **Done** is in the **center**, with **no constriction**.
children: It is the open shape that the other vowels are compared with.

teaching.text: Each label describes a different feature.
children: High or low tells how high the tongue is.
Front or back tells where the tongue sits in the mouth.
The fraction tells how far along the air path the narrowing is.

teaching.text: The place of narrowing links the mouth to the sound.
children: Narrowing the airway changes how the air behaves at that spot.
Each formant then shifts according to how its mode moves and squeezes the air there.

teaching.text: A chain gains one more **normal mode** for every mass that can move. A chain of one mass has one mode, and a chain of six masses has six.

teaching.text: The size of a movement and the rate of a movement are different things.

This is the lowest mode, and its frequency is the **fundamental**.

teaching.text: The next shape fits **two half-waves**.

children: The vocal folds vibrate at a **fundamental frequency**, called **F0**.
They also produce **harmonics** at every whole-number multiple of F0.
In this example, the harmonics are **100 Hz** apart.
Before the vocal tract acts, these harmonics are evenly spaced and all the same strength.

teaching.text: The filter **changes the strength** of each harmonic.
children: The vocal tract has its own resonances, called **formants**.
Harmonics close to a formant become stronger. Harmonics far from a formant become weaker.
The harmonics stay at the same frequencies. Only their strengths change.

teaching.text: The overall pattern of strengths is called the **spectral envelope**.
children: The envelope is what makes a vowel sound like that vowel.

teaching.text: Two terms that are easy to mix up are kept apart here.
children: **F0** is how fast the vocal folds repeat.
**F1** is the lowest resonance of the vocal tract.
A vowel is made of many harmonics. The formants decide which of them are strong.

sections.title: The /i/ filter keeps F1 low and F2 high

teaching.text: For **/i/**, the vocal tract keeps **F1 low** and makes **F2 high**. It works on the same 100 Hz comb from the source.
children: There is a group of strong harmonics near the low end.
The next strong group is much higher up.
Between them, the harmonics are weak.

teaching.text: The harmonics themselves do not move.
children: They keep the same even spacing.
Only their strengths change, and that change is what the filter does.

teaching.text: This pattern comes from where /i/ narrows the tract.
children: At the narrowing, the first mode moves the air a lot. The extra mass lowers F1.
At the same spot, the second mode squeezes the air a lot. The extra stiffness raises F2.
So F1 and F2 end up far apart, which is what makes /i/ sound like /i/.

teaching.text: Each harmonic has two separate properties.
children: Its **frequency** is where it sits.
Its **amplitude** is how strong it is.
A strong harmonic at a low frequency is still a low-frequency harmonic.

sections.title: The /a/ filter raises F1 and lowers F2

teaching.text: For **/a/**, the vocal tract does the reverse of /i/. **F1 goes up**, and **F2 comes down**. This brings the first two formants close together.
children: In this example, **F1** is at **750 Hz**, and **F2** is near **1200 Hz**.
The source is the same as before. Only the shape of the tract has changed, and that alone makes a different vowel.

teaching.text: A formant does not have to line up with a harmonic.
children: The F1 of 750 Hz falls between the harmonics at **700** and **800 Hz**.
Those two nearby harmonics become strong because they are close to the formant.
But no new harmonic appears at 750 Hz. The filter can only change the strength of harmonics the source already has.

teaching.text: A formant and a harmonic are different things.
children: A **formant** is a resonance of the vocal tract. It belongs to the filter.
A **harmonic** is a frequency made by the vocal folds. It belongs to the source.
The filter decides how strong each harmonic is. The harmonics, in turn, reveal where the formants are.

sections.title: A spectrogram places successive spectra in time

teaching.text: A **spectrum** shows the sound at **one moment**. A **spectrogram** lines up **many spectra over time**, so it tracks how the sound changes.
A spectrum gives the strength of each frequency during one short slice of sound.
children: Taking several slices of **/i/** and then several of **/a/** gives a series of spectra.

teaching.text: A spectrogram puts those slices side by side.
children: Time runs from left to right.
Frequency runs from bottom to top.
**Darker** marks mean **stronger** sound, and lighter marks mean weaker sound.

teaching.text: This makes two kinds of change easy to tell apart.
children: When a band gets darker, that frequency is getting stronger.
When a band moves up, the formant is moving to a higher frequency.
Moving to the right always means later in time, not higher in frequency.

teaching.text: As **/i/** changes into **/a/**, **F1 rises** and **F2 falls**.
children: The two lowest bands move toward each other.
The spectrogram follows the changing shape of the vocal tract over time, which a single spectrum cannot do.

sections.title: Reflection prompt
Wide harmonic spacing makes formants harder to identify

teaching.text: Formants can only be seen through the harmonics. The filter can only change the strength of frequencies that the source provides. So how clearly a formant shows up depends on how close together the harmonics are.
When harmonics are **close together**, formants are easy to see.
children: With harmonics every **100 Hz**, many harmonics fall near each formant.
Their strengths rise toward the center of the formant and fall on either side.
This traces the shape of the formant clearly.

teaching.text: When **F0** goes up, the harmonics spread apart.
children: With harmonics every **250 Hz**, far fewer harmonics fall near each formant.
A formant can fall between two harmonics, so no harmonic sits at its center.
It becomes very hard to tell harmonics and formants apart.

teaching.text: Some voices make this even harder.
children: A **toddler** has a high voice, so the harmonics could be **400 Hz** apart.
A **soprano** sings even higher, with harmonics that could be **800 Hz** apart.
With so few harmonics, the formants are very hard to read.

teaching.text: The vocal tract has not changed in these cases.
children: Its formants are in the same places.
Only the source has changed. A higher voice gives fewer harmonics, and fewer harmonics give a less clear picture of the same formants.

sections.title: Homework 4 lab reminder
Speech → Neural Networks
Five membrane modes combine into one motion

teaching.text: A **membrane** is a vibrating surface with fixed edges. A surface spreads in two directions, so each mode is named with two numbers. Each number counts the moving regions in one direction.
children: In **(1,1)**, the whole surface moves as one region.
In **(2,1)** and **(1,2)**, the surface splits into two regions, in one direction or the other.
In **(2,2)**, it splits into four regions, and in **(3,1)**, into three in a row.

teaching.text: Regions that sit next to each other always move in opposite directions.
children: The lines between them stay still. These still lines are **nodes**.
The outer edges stay still too, because they are fixed.

teaching.text: All the modes can happen at once, and their movements add at every point.
children: Some places build up and others cancel, so the whole surface keeps changing shape.

teaching.text: A node stays still the whole time.
children: A moving region also passes through the flat resting level, but only for an instant on its way past. That passing moment does not make it a node.
The two numbers describe how the surface divides. They are not two separate frequencies.

teaching.text: A **pickup** at one point gives a spectrum with one peak for each mode.
children: The frequencies here were **picked for teaching** and spaced evenly. A real rectangle would have its own natural frequencies, so the even spacing models how frequencies combine rather than how every membrane behaves.

sections.title: A fixed end and a free end select odd harmonics

teaching.text: A **fixed–free system** is held at one end and free at the other. Each end sets a rule for every shape the system can take.
children: The fixed end must be a **node**, a point that does not move.
The free end must be an **antinode**, the point that moves the most.

teaching.text: The shapes that follow both rules fit odd numbers of **quarter-waves**.
children: The simplest shape fits one quarter-wave. It is still at the fixed end and swings most at the free end.
The next shapes fit three, five and seven quarter-waves.
These are the **first, third, fifth and seventh harmonics**. So the second allowed mode is the third harmonic, not the second.

teaching.text: Even numbers of quarter-waves are not allowed.
children: An even number would put a still point at the free end, which breaks the rule for that end.
Higher modes fit shorter waves into the same length, so they repeat faster.

teaching.text: The antinode does not stay at its farthest point.
children: It swings through rest to the other side on each cycle.
The fixed end stays still the whole time.

teaching.text: The fixed–fixed and fixed–free examples were tuned separately to share the same lowest frequency.
children: If only one end were freed, with nothing else changed, the lowest frequency would drop **by half**.

sections.title: Quarter-wavelength packets explain the allowed modes

teaching.text: A **quarter-wavelength** is the part of a standing wave that goes from a **node**, where nothing moves, to an **antinode**, where movement is greatest. A fixed–free string needs a node at its fixed bottom and an antinode at its free top.
children: One quarter-wave fits between those two ends.
This is the simplest pattern, and it gives the lowest frequency.

teaching.text: The next pattern cannot add just one quarter-wave.
children: One more would end the string on a node.
A free end cannot be a node, so that pattern is not allowed.

teaching.text: Adding **two** quarter-waves works.
children: It brings the top back to an antinode.
So the allowed patterns have **one, three, five and seven** quarter-waves.

teaching.text: More pieces in the same length make the waves shorter.
children: Shorter waves repeat faster.
So each allowed pattern has a higher frequency than the one before.

teaching.text: The four patterns line up with the **odd harmonics**.
children: Only odd numbers of quarter-waves start at a node and end at an antinode.
The even harmonics are missing because the two ends of the string rule them out.

sections.title: Air moves longitudinally in vocal-tract modes

teaching.text: The air in the vocal tract can be pictured as a chain of masses joined by springs.
children: Moving air has **inertia**, so it tends to keep moving. That is the mass.
Squeezed air pushes back. That is the spring.
The air moves **back and forth** along the tube, around its usual place. It does not stream steadily out of the mouth.

teaching.text: The tube has one fixed end and one free end.
children: The **glottis** is the fixed end, where the air has little room to move.
The open **lips** are the free end, where the air moves most easily.

teaching.text: The two slowest patterns of this tube match the first two formants.
children: **Mode 1 is like F1**, the lowest resonance.
**Mode 2 is like F2**, with one more back-and-forth reversal inside the tube.
In a perfectly even tube, Mode 2 runs **three times** as fast as Mode 1. A different tube shape changes that.

teaching.text: Each mode is one pattern of motion shared by the whole column of air.
children: In some places, neighboring bits of air move together.
In other places, the gaps between them keep opening and closing.

teaching.text: Three vowels narrow the tube at three places.
children: **/a/** narrows it about **one-third** of the way up from the glottis.
**/i/** narrows it about **two-thirds** of the way up.
**/u/** narrows it at the **lips**.
Mass matters where a mode moves, and springiness matters where it squeezes. So one narrowing can push F1 and F2 in different directions.

sections.title: Track air motion separately from compression

teaching.text: Each spot in a vibrating column of air can be described in two ways.
children: **Movement** is how far the air at that spot travels.
**Compression** is how much the gaps between neighboring bits of air change.

teaching.text: These are two different things.
children: A group of air can travel a long way together while the gaps between them stay the same.
In other places, the gaps squeeze and stretch a lot around air that barely moves.

teaching.text: Each is found in its own way.
children: To find movement, follow one bit of air through a full cycle.
To find compression, watch the gaps around it open and close.

teaching.text: Together, they keep the air vibrating.
children: Squeezed air pushes back. That is the spring.
Moving air keeps going. That is the mass.

teaching.text: The closed end of the tube holds the air still, and the open end lets it move.
children: Each mode places its moving and squeezing regions in different spots.
So a narrowing in one place can affect moving mass in one mode and squeezing in another.
What a narrowing does depends on both the mode and the place.

sections.title: Compare positions within an air mode

teaching.text: This **pop quiz** marks six spots along the air column and asks what each spot is doing.
children: Each spot must be followed through a **full cycle**.
How far its air travels gives its movement.
How the gaps around it change gives its compression.
One still picture is not enough, because air that moves a lot can look still for a moment as it passes through rest.

teaching.text: Where the air **moves a lot**, added mass matters.
children: Extra mass is harder to get moving and harder to stop.
The cycle takes longer, so the frequency **goes down**.

teaching.text: Where the air is **squeezed a lot**, added stiffness matters.
children: Extra stiffness pushes the air back harder.
The cycle gets shorter, so the frequency **goes up**.

teaching.text: Each mode puts its moving and squeezing spots in different places.
children: A spot that moves a lot in one mode can be squeezed a lot in another.
So predicting the effect of a narrowing takes two things, the **place** and the **mode**.

sections.title: Vowel positions change where the tract is narrowed

teaching.text: Vowels are usually described by **tongue height** and by whether the tongue is **front or back**. Each vowel also narrows the airway at one particular place.
The two high vowels narrow the airway in different places.
children: **Dean** is **high and front**. It narrows about **two-thirds** of the way from the glottis to the lips.
**Dune** is **high and back**. It narrows at the **lips**.
They are both high, but their tract shapes are different.

teaching.text: The two low vowels are at the bottom.
children: **Dan** is **low and front**.
**Don** is **low and back**. It narrows about **one-third** of the way from the glottis.

teaching.text: **Done** is in the **center**, with **no constriction**.
children: It is the open shape that the other vowels are compared with.

teaching.text: Each label describes a different feature.
children: High or low tells how high the tongue is.
Front or back tells where the tongue sits in the mouth.
The fraction tells how far along the air path the narrowing is.

teaching.text: The place of narrowing links the mouth to the sound.
children: Narrowing the airway changes how the air behaves at that spot.
Each formant then shifts according to how its mode moves and squeezes the air there.

sections.title: A constriction changes inertia and restoring stiffness

teaching.text: A **constriction** narrows the air passage. Narrowing changes two things about the air at that spot.
First, the air becomes **stiffer**.
children: Squeezed air pushes back harder.
Where a mode squeezes the air a lot, this extra stiffness makes the mode faster. The frequency **goes up**.

teaching.text: Second, the air gains **mass**.
children: Bunched-up air is denser.
Where a mode moves the air a lot, this extra mass makes the mode slower. The frequency **goes down**.

teaching.text: A constriction adds both mass and stiffness, but they do not simply cancel.
children: The places where air **moves the most** take turns with the places where air is **squeezed the most**.
Each mode puts these places in different spots.
So one spot can be a moving place for one mode and a squeezing place for another.

teaching.text: To see which effect wins, the air must be followed through a full cycle.
children: How far one bit of air travels reveals the moving mass.
How the gaps around it open and close reveals the squeezing.

teaching.text: So one constriction can work mainly through **mass** for one formant and mainly through **stiffness** for another.
children: One formant goes down, and the other goes up.
The rules stay the same. Mass lowers frequency where air moves, and stiffness raises it where air is squeezed.

sections.title: Use both modes to interpret the same tract location

teaching.text: **Mode 1** and **Mode 2** are two ways that the same column of air can vibrate. The column is closed at the glottis and open at the lips.
children: Both modes move the air a lot near the lips.
Mode 2 has one more back-and-forth reversal inside the tube, so its moving and squeezing spots are in different places.

teaching.text: Three places are marked along the tube, at the **back**, the **front** and the **lips**.
children: Each place is the same spot in both modes.
Narrowing the tube at one place changes the air there for both modes.

teaching.text: What the narrowing does depends on what each mode is doing at that spot.
children: If a mode **moves** the air there a lot, the added mass slows it down.
If a mode **squeezes** the air there a lot, the added stiffness speeds it up.
The two modes can be doing different things at the same spot. So one narrowing can push **F1** and **F2** in opposite directions.

teaching.text: **Formants** and **harmonics** are different things.
children: Formants are resonances of the vocal tract. They change when the shape of the tract changes.
Harmonics come from the vocal folds. Their spacing changes when the pitch changes.

sections.title: Lip loading lowers both F1 and F2 in the /u/ model

teaching.text: For **/u/**, the lips are rounded and narrowed. This is the **free end** of the air column, and narrowing it adds more **effective mass**, which means more air has to be moved back and forth at the lips.
Both of the lowest modes move strongly at the lips.
children: In **Mode 1**, **motion dominates** at the lips.
In **Mode 2**, **motion dominates** at the lips too.

teaching.text: A heavier moving load is slower to speed up and slower to turn around.
children: Each cycle takes longer.
Both modes slow down, so **F1 goes down and F2 goes down**.

teaching.text: The two modes are shaped differently inside the tube.
children: But they both swing strongly at the lips, so the extra load slows both of them.
F1 is still the lower formant, and F2 is still the higher one.

teaching.text: Both formants fall because the lips play the same role in both modes.
children: In both, the air at the lips mostly moves.
Narrowing in other places can work differently, so this is not true of every narrowing.

sections.title: A front constriction separates the effects on F1 and F2

teaching.text: For **/i/**, the tongue narrows the airway near the front, about **two-thirds** of the way from the glottis to the lips. It is one spot, but that spot plays a different part in each mode.
In **Mode 1**, **mass motion dominates** at that spot.
children: The air there swings a lot in this mode.
Narrowing it adds moving mass, and moving mass is slow to turn around.
The mode slows down, so **F1 goes down**.

teaching.text: In **Mode 2**, **springiness dominates** at that same spot.
children: The air there is squeezed and stretched a lot in this mode.
Narrowing it makes the air push back harder.
The mode speeds up, so **F2 goes up**.

teaching.text: The spot stays in the same place. What changes is its job in each mode.
children: Where the air mostly swings, added mass matters most.
Where the air mostly squeezes, added springiness matters most.

teaching.text: So **/i/** has a **lower F1 and a higher F2** than the even tube.
children: The two effects do not cancel each other out.
Each mode follows the effect that is stronger at that spot in its own pattern.

sections.title: A back constriction reverses the F1 and F2 pattern

teaching.text: For **/a/**, the narrowing is farther back, about **one-third** of the way up from the glottis. At this spot, the two modes switch the roles they had for /i/.
In **Mode 1**, **springiness dominates** at this spot.
children: The air here is squeezed and stretched a lot in this mode.
Narrowing it makes the air push back harder, so the mode speeds up and **F1 goes up**.

teaching.text: In **Mode 2**, **mass motion dominates** at this spot.
children: The air here swings a lot in this mode.
Narrowing it adds moving mass, so the mode slows down and **F2 goes down**.

teaching.text: One spot can have two different jobs.
children: In one job, the spot barely moves, but the air on each side crowds in and spreads out. That is squeezing.
In the other job, the spot moves a lot, but the gaps around it stay about the same. That is swinging.
At the one-third point, Mode 1 gives the spot a squeezing job, and Mode 2 gives it a swinging job.

teaching.text: So **/a/** has a **higher F1 and a lower F2**, the reverse of /i/.
children: Moving the narrowing changes which job each mode gives it.
Mass and stiffness still work the same way they always do.

sections.title: Air motion and compression in the vocal-tract modes

teaching.text: Every spot in a vibrating column of air can be described in two ways, by its **movement** and by its **compression**.
children: **Movement** is how far a bit of air travels.
**Compression** is how the gaps between neighboring bits change. When the gaps shrink, the air is **compressed**. When they grow, the air is **thinned out**, which is called **rarefaction**.

teaching.text: These are two different things.
children: Neighbors can travel a long way together while their gaps stay the same.
Neighbors can also crowd together and spread apart around a bit of air that barely moves.

teaching.text: Movement and compression act like a mass and a spring.
children: Crowded air pushes back toward its normal spacing. That is the spring.
Moving air keeps going because of inertia. That is the mass.
Together, they keep the air moving back and forth around its usual place.

teaching.text: Each higher mode fits more alternating stretches of movement and compression into the same tube.
children: Where movement is large, there is a lot of moving mass.
Where the gaps change a lot, there is strong push-back.
These places are different in each mode.

teaching.text: This tells where a narrowing will matter.
children: Added mass matters most where the air moves a lot.
Added stiffness matters most where the air is squeezed a lot.
Each mode is a separate resonance of the same air, not a separate stream of air.

sections.title: The vocal-fold source sets harmonic spacing

teaching.text: The vocal folds make the **source** of a voiced sound. How fast they repeat is called **F0**, and F0 sets how far apart the harmonics are.
A **vibrating membrane** gives a model for this.
children: Its modes combine into one motion with evenly spaced frequencies.
That even spacing is what a harmonic source looks like.

teaching.text: Different vocal folds give different spacing.
children: Heavy, loose vocal folds repeat slowly. Their harmonics are **close together**.
Tighter, lighter vocal folds repeat faster. With an F0 of **250 Hz**, the harmonics are 250 Hz apart.
Very tight, light vocal folds repeat faster still. With an F0 of **350 Hz**, the harmonics are 350 Hz apart.

teaching.text: This follows the same rule as every oscillator.
children: More mass makes the vibration slower.
More tension makes it faster.

teaching.text: A voiced vowel is made of **many frequencies** at once.
children: The source decides which harmonics are present.
The vocal tract then makes some of them stronger and others weaker.
So pitch and vowel shape change two different parts of the same sound.

sections.title: The vocal-tract filter favors nearby harmonics

teaching.text: The vocal tract acts as a **filter**. It is like a tube that is closed at one end and open at the other. Its resonances are called **formants**, and they follow one simple rule.
children: **A formant makes the harmonics closest to it louder.**
**Harmonics far from any formant are made quieter.**
The source supplies the harmonics. The filter decides which ones come through strongly.

teaching.text: Each vowel puts its formants in different places.
children: **Schwa** has its first two formants well apart.
**/u/** has both of them low.
**/i/** has a low first formant and a very high second formant.
**/a/** has its first two formants close together.

teaching.text: Changing the shape of the tongue and lips changes the shape of the tract.
children: That moves the formants.
So the shape of the vowel is the filter.

teaching.text: A formant and a harmonic are not the same thing.
children: A formant is a resonance of the vocal tract.
A harmonic is a frequency that comes from the vocal folds.
A formant can fall between two harmonics and still make both of them louder. The filter changes the strength of harmonics, but it does not create new ones.

sections.title: One filter can look different at different pitches

teaching.text: The same vowel can look different at different pitches. Comparing one vowel at several pitches separates what the voice does from what the vocal tract does.
When only the **pitch** changes, the formants stay in the same place.
children: The harmonics spread farther apart as the pitch goes up.

teaching.text: When only the **vowel** changes, the harmonics stay in the same place.
children: The formants move.

teaching.text: **Close-together harmonics trace a formant well.**
children: At a low pitch, many harmonics fall near each formant.
Their strengths rise and fall smoothly, showing the shape of the formant clearly.

teaching.text: **Spread-out harmonics can hide a formant.**
children: At a high pitch, only a few harmonics fall near each formant.
A strong harmonic might sit next to a formant instead of right on it.
Two formants that are close together, like the first two in /a/, can blur into what looks like one.

teaching.text: A formant that is hard to see is still there.
children: The vocal tract has not changed.
Only the voice has changed, and a higher voice gives fewer harmonics to reveal the same formants.

sections.title: Map spectra into a spectrogram

teaching.text: A **spectrum** shows the sound at **one moment**. A **spectrogram** lines up **many spectra over time**.
Two changes turn a series of spectra into a spectrogram.
children: First, each spectrum is turned on its side, so frequency runs from bottom to top. The spectra are then placed side by side in time order.
Second, the strength of each frequency is shown as **darkness**. Darker means stronger.

teaching.text: This makes two kinds of change easy to see.
children: A band that moves **up** is moving to a higher frequency.
A band that gets **darker** is getting stronger.

teaching.text: The left-to-right direction means different things in the two pictures.
children: In a spectrum, moving right means higher frequency.
In a spectrogram, moving right means later in time.

teaching.text: As **/i/** changes to **/a/**, the first formant **rises** and the second formant **falls**.
children: The two bands move toward each other.
The spectrogram tracks how the vocal tract changes over time.

sections.title: Reflection prompt
Speech-complexity experiment prompt
Use formants as input to vowel recognition

teaching.text: All of this connects back to **AI**. The plan is to build a **neural network** that learns from students’ **formants** and decides which vowel is being spoken.
The network uses two numbers, **F1** and **F2**.
children: These are the first two formants of the vowel.
Two numbers are enough to start with, because the position of the tongue and lips moves these two formants in typical ways for each vowel.

teaching.text: The **input** and the **output** are different kinds of information.
children: The input is the pair of formant measurements.
The output is a choice among vowel categories.
To learn, the network needs to know the true vowel for each example.

teaching.text: This links the physics of speech with machine learning.
children: The mass–spring model explains where F1 and F2 come from.
The network learns how those two numbers match up with each vowel.
Training and testing will reveal how well it learns.

sections.title: A fully connected linear vowel network

teaching.text: The vowel network is a **purely linear** network. It takes **2 inputs**, passes them through **three hidden layers**, and ends with **5 outputs**, one for each word. It uses **no activation functions**.
The two inputs are **F1** and **F2**.
Every layer is **fully connected**.
children: Each neuron is connected to every neuron in the layer before it.
Each connection has a **weight**. A weight is a number that sets how much that connection counts.
A neuron multiplies each incoming value by its weight and adds them all up. That total is its value.

teaching.text: The **hidden layers** hold in-between results.
children: Each hidden value is a new mix of the values that came before.
Each neuron has its own weights, so each one mixes the inputs in its own way.

teaching.text: The five outputs stand for five words, **done**, **dune**, **dean**, **Don** and **Dan**.
**Purely linear** means each layer just adds up weighted values and passes them on.
children: Nothing in between bends or reshapes the numbers.
So the whole network is a chain of weighted sums.
On its own, that chain does not turn the outputs into probabilities.

sections.title: Random weights assign signed contributions to connections

teaching.text: One example goes into the network, with **F1 at 320** and **F2 at 2000**. Before training, **every connection gets a random weight**.
The input and the weights do different jobs.
children: The input **measures** the sound.
The weights are the network’s **settings**. They decide how the measurements get mixed together.
If the weights change, every result inside the network changes, even with the same input.

teaching.text: Each neuron mixes its inputs in its own way.
children: It multiplies each incoming value by a weight and adds up the results.
The first neurons each get F1 and F2, but each one has its own two weights, so each one makes a different mix.

teaching.text: Before training, **every weight is a random number between −1 and 1**.
children: Some weights are **positive**, and some are **negative**.
A negative weight flips the sign of its input.
So some contributions add up, and others cancel each other out.

teaching.text: These random weights hold no knowledge about vowels yet.
children: Sending an example through the network with its current weights is called a **forward pass**.
**Learning** is what changes the weights so the network gets better.

sections.title: Forward flow and an illustrative output distribution

teaching.text: In a **forward pass**, the input moves through the network **one layer at a time**. At the end, the network gives a **probability for each of the five words**.
Each layer mixes the values from the layer before and passes them on.
children: This continues until the output layer is reached.
Learning is a separate step that changes the weights.

teaching.text: In the example, the network gives **done** the highest probability, **0.5**.
children: **Dan** gets 0.2.
Each of the other three words gets 0.1.
So the network’s best guess is **done**.

teaching.text: Probabilities follow two rules.
children: Each one is between zero and one.
Together, they add up to one.

teaching.text: The example output pictures the kind of result the network should give.
children: A purely linear network has no step that makes sure its outputs follow these rules.

teaching.text: A **predicted** answer is not the same as a **true** answer.
children: The predicted answer is the word the network favors.
The true answer is the vowel that was really spoken.
Only the true answer can say whether the network was right.

sections.title: Declare the layer sequence in PyTorch

teaching.text: The same network can be written in **PyTorch**, a tool for building neural networks.
The code first loads PyTorch and its neural-network tools, called **nn**.
children: The network itself is stored under the name **net**.

teaching.text: **nn.Sequential** stacks the layers in order.
children: Information passes through the layers in the order they are listed.

teaching.text: Each layer is written as **nn.Linear**, followed by two numbers.
children: The first number is how many values come in.
The second number is how many values go out.
The layers go from 2 to 3, then 3 to 2, then 2 to 4, then 4 to 5.
The number going out of each layer matches the number coming into the next one, so the values can flow all the way through.

teaching.text: Each layer also says **bias=False**.
children: A bias is an extra number that a layer can add to each sum.
Turning it off keeps every layer purely linear, just like the picture.
All the weights are still there, and they can still be learned.

teaching.text: This code only **describes** the network.
children: It does not train it.
Training would need examples with the right answers, and a way to change the weights.

lecture15.title: Neural Networks · Forward propagation, learning, and sigmoid

sections.title: Neural Networks
Two formants feed a fully connected network

teaching.text: The vowel network takes in two numbers, **F1** and **F2**. It gives back one response for each of five words, **done**, **dune**, **dean**, **Don** and **Dan**.
children: The inputs are measurements of the sound.
The outputs are the network’s responses to each word.

teaching.text: Between the inputs and outputs are three **hidden layers**.
children: They hold three, two and four neurons.
Each hidden neuron takes values from the layer before it and passes its result to the next layer.

teaching.text: Every layer is **fully connected**.
children: Each neuron is wired to every neuron in the next layer.
Each wire has its own **weight**.
A weight sets how much the value on that wire counts. A positive weight keeps its sign, and a negative weight flips it.

teaching.text: F1 and F2 both feed every neuron in the first hidden layer.
children: Each of those wires has a different weight.
So each first-layer neuron mixes the same two formants in its own way.

teaching.text: Changing a formant and changing a weight are two different things.
children: A new formant changes what travels along the wires.
A new weight changes how much a wire counts.
A weight is never the probability of a word.

sections.title: Forward propagation combines weighted inputs

teaching.text: **Forward propagation** carries the input through the network, one layer at a time. The example uses **F1 = 320** and **F2 = 2000**.
The first neuron multiplies each input by its weight and adds the results.
children: Its weight for F1 is small and positive. Its weight for F2 is small and negative.
F2’s negative part is larger, so the total comes out to **−0.40**.

teaching.text: Multiplying and then adding like this is called an **inner product**.
children: The other neurons do the same thing with their own weights.
A negative result is still an ordinary number that the next layer can use.

teaching.text: Each layer repeats this step on the results of the layer before it.
children: The layers have to go in order, because each one needs the results of the last.

teaching.text: The final sums are called **logits**. They are scores, not probabilities.
children: A step called **softmax** turns them into probabilities.
Softmax makes every probability positive, and it makes them all add up to 1.

teaching.text: For this example, the network gives **done** the highest probability, about **56%**.
children: It gives **dean** only about **8%**.
These are just the network’s current guesses. They do not tell which word was really spoken.

sections.title: Pop quiz · Forward propagation
Info on Exam 2 and Exam 3
Backpropagation uses the difference between prediction and target

teaching.text: **Backpropagation** is how a network learns. It starts by comparing the network’s answer with the right answer.
The network’s answer is its **computed output**.
children: For the example, it favors **done**.
It gives **dean** only about **8%**.

teaching.text: The right answer is the **desired output**.
children: It marks **dean** as the correct word, because dean was the word that was spoken.
So the network’s best guess and the right answer do not match.

teaching.text: A **loss** puts a number on how wrong the network is.
children: The loss used here, **cross-entropy**, looks at the probability given to the true word.
More probability on dean means a smaller loss. Less probability means a larger loss.

teaching.text: The calculation then works **backward**.
children: It starts at the outputs and figures out how the last layer of weights caused the error.
It uses that result to work out the layer before, and so on, back to the start.

teaching.text: A **gradient** tells how the loss would change if one weight changed a little.
children: Each weight is then moved a small step in the direction that lowers the loss.
A positive gradient makes the weight go down. A negative gradient makes it go up.

teaching.text: All the weights are updated together in one step.
children: After the update, the network has to be run forward again to see its new answers.

sections.title: Predict how changing a marked weight affects error

teaching.text: The question is, **if this weight goes up, does the error go up or down?** The right word is **dean**, but the network favors **done**. So the real question is what the change does to dean’s probability.
One marked weight connects the last hidden layer directly to **done**.
children: The weight is positive, and the value coming into it is positive.
Raising this weight raises the score for done.
The five probabilities share one total, so a higher score for done leaves less for dean.
The error goes **up**, so this weight should come down.

teaching.text: Another marked weight sits at the very start, connecting **F1** to the first hidden layer.
children: Raising it changes that first neuron’s value.
That change then spreads through every later layer and reaches all five words.
Looking at this one early weight is not enough to know which way the error will move.

teaching.text: Working backward through every layer gives the answer.
children: For this example, raising the early weight also makes the error go up.
So both weights should come down.
The weight near the output was easy to judge. The early weight needed every path after it added together, and that adding up is what backpropagation does.

sections.title: Backpropagation reuses downstream error calculations

teaching.text: Why does training run **backward**? The answer comes from comparing the **last** weights with the **first** weights.
The **last weights** sit right next to the output.
children: They set the output probabilities directly.
So the error depends on them very directly.
The gap between the network’s answer and the right answer shows right away how to improve them.

teaching.text: The **first weights** sit far from the output.
children: They shape the first layer, which then passes through two more layers before reaching the output.
It is hard to tell how much of the final mistake they caused.
Their effect also includes the effect of the last weights, since the last weights come after them.

teaching.text: So fixing the last weights is the **easy** problem.
children: Fixing the first weights depends on it.

teaching.text: A good way to handle problems like this is to solve the small ones first and then reuse their answers for the big ones.
children: This method is called **dynamic programming**.
**Backpropagation** is a form of dynamic programming. It works out the effects near the output first, saves them, and reuses them for each earlier layer.

teaching.text: In short, **backpropagation** combines two ideas.
children: **SGD**, stochastic gradient descent, is the rule that adjusts each weight.
Dynamic programming is what makes the gradients for SGD quick to compute.

sections.title: Pair each recording with its target row

teaching.text: To learn, the network needs many examples, each with the right answer attached. These are stored in two **training matrices**.
The first matrix holds the **inputs**.
children: It has **110 rows**, one for each recording.
Each row holds that recording’s **F1** and **F2**.

teaching.text: The second matrix holds the **right answers**.
children: It also has 110 rows, one for each recording.
It has five columns, one for each word.
Each row puts a **1** under the correct word and a **0** under the other four. This is called a **one-hot** target.

teaching.text: For example, the recording with **F1 = 320** and **F2 = 2000** is marked as **dean**.
children: This is the same example that went through the network.

teaching.text: The rows of the two matrices must stay lined up.
children: Each row of formants must stay next to the right answer for that same recording.
If they got out of order, the network would learn from the wrong answers.

teaching.text: The network’s guess and the right answer are kept separate.
children: Before training, the network guesses **done** for the dean recording.
The answer matrix still says **dean**. Training compares the two and moves the network toward the right answer.

sections.title: Read one full-batch training step in PyTorch

teaching.text: One full step of training can be written in a short **PyTorch** program. It uses all **110 recordings** at once.
The program first loads the two matrices.
children: **X** holds the formants for each recording.
**Y** holds the right answer for each recording.

teaching.text: Then it builds the network, layer by layer, with **nn.Sequential**.
children: The layers have the same sizes as the network in the picture.
No sigmoid is used between the layers yet.

teaching.text: Then come the training lines.
children: **SGD** is set up with a **learning rate of 0.1**. The learning rate sets how big each step is.
**zero_grad** clears out any old gradients.
The **loss** line runs the network on the data and measures how wrong it is.
**backward** works out the gradient for every weight.
**step** uses those gradients to change the weights.

teaching.text: Each of these lines does a separate job.
children: Working out a gradient does not change a weight by itself. Only the step does that.

teaching.text: This program takes just **one** step, with no loop to repeat it.
children: It also starts from PyTorch’s own random weights. So it has the same shape as the network in the picture, but not the same numbers.

sections.title: Sigmoid turns an inner product into a bounded activation

teaching.text: The **sigmoid** function takes an inner product and turns it into a number between **0 and 1**. Its formula is **σ(z) = 1 / (1 + exp(−z))**.
Big numbers get pushed close to the ends.
children: If the inner product is **large and positive**, the sigmoid is close to **1**.
If it is **large and negative**, the sigmoid is close to **0**.
For example, an input of **4** gives about **0.98**, and an input of **−4** gives about **0.02**.

teaching.text: The sigmoid has an S shape.
children: It is steep in the middle. A small change there makes a big change in the output.
It is flat at both ends. A big change there makes only a small change in the output.

teaching.text: The idea comes from biology.
children: **Lord Edgar Adrian** won the **Nobel Prize** in 1932 for work on nerve cells.
In his view, **neurons are nearly digital**, either on or off, roughly.
The sigmoid captures this. It acts almost like an on-off switch at its ends, but it changes smoothly in the middle.

teaching.text: **Animal perception** works in a similar way.
children: Some things that seem alike are perceived as different.
Some things that are very different are perceived as the same.
The sigmoid does the same thing. Two inputs on either side of the steep middle come out very different, while two inputs far out on one end come out almost the same.

sections.title: Apply sigmoid while recalculating downstream activity

teaching.text: Sigmoid can be added to the network **one neuron at a time**. The input stays the same, and the weights stay the same.
When the first neuron switches to sigmoid, its output changes from **−0.40** to about **0.40**.
children: That new value changes what every later neuron receives.
So every later value has to be worked out again, all the way to the output.
Adding sigmoid to one neuron changes the whole rest of the network.

teaching.text: The process continues until every hidden neuron uses sigmoid.
children: Each hidden value is now squeezed between 0 and 1.

teaching.text: The output still uses **softmax** to turn scores into probabilities.
children: With sigmoid in every hidden neuron, the network now favors **Dan**, at about **32%**.
**Dean** rises to about **23%**, up from about 8%.
**Done** drops from first place to about 16%.

teaching.text: The input and the weights never changed.
children: Only the activation rule changed, yet the network’s answers changed a lot.

teaching.text: This is not learning.
children: Dean’s probability went up, but Dan is still the top guess.
Adding sigmoid can change the network’s favorite word, but only training can teach it the right one.

sections.title: Insert sigmoid after the hidden linear layers

teaching.text: The PyTorch program for the sigmoid network is the same as before, with one change. **nn.Sigmoid()** is added after each hidden layer.
Each hidden layer now does two things.
children: First, it adds up its weighted inputs.
Then it passes those sums through sigmoid before sending them on.

teaching.text: Sigmoid changes each value, but it does not change how many values there are.
children: A layer that gives out three values still gives out three values after sigmoid.
So each next layer still receives the right number of inputs.

teaching.text: The very last layer has **no** sigmoid after it.
children: Its five scores go straight to the loss, which turns them into probabilities.
The hidden sigmoids and the final probabilities do different jobs. No hidden neuron stands for a word.

teaching.text: The training lines are exactly the same.
children: Clear the old gradients, run the network and measure the loss, work out the gradients, then take a step.
The learning rate is still **0.1**, and all 110 recordings are used in the one step.

teaching.text: The program starts from PyTorch’s own random weights.
children: So it has the same shape as the network in the picture.
It would only give the same probabilities if it started from the same weights.
